articles.title: Nvidia Board Revolts Over Secret Disclosures and SEC Probes
articles.content: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story Jensen Huang was ousted from Nvidia amid allegations of extramarital affairs , including a relationship with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset. Yet it was “multiple issues” related to Huang’s “lack of candor” and “lying” that ultimately moved the board of directors , according to two people familiar with private discussions among the chair and other members. While Huang admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang on November 8, the board couldn’t determine in the moment whether she was an intelligence operative for China, these sources say. That same day, the board announced an independent investigation “in light of recent reporting” that their CEO had “been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.” China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has rejected allegations that Alice Huang was a spy. But in the following days, once allegations of other affairs surfaced, including one reportedly with a direct report, “what could be determined was [Huang’s] lying, and that spanned a year, from October 2025 through recent events,” a source close to the board told WIRED, who requested anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak on its behalf. According to sources, members of the board had asked Huang about Alice Huang after The New York Times first reported in October 2025 that Nvidia had an unusually robust business relationship with a Singapore-based data center company named Megaspeed, where Alice Huang had worked. Jensen Huang at the time denied any inappropriate relationship with Alice Huang to the board, sources tell WIRED. After the affair came to light, the board was incensed, these people say. A source familiar with the board’s thinking told WIRED that while these board members view issues of national security as “important” and “ongoing,” the primary driver behind Huang’s ouster was “the lying.” “It was a matter of integrity and trust,” this person said. In recent days, board members, including chair Harvey Jones, have tried to quell the discourse about Huang’s possible return to Nvidia by emphasizing that Huang's behavior flew in the face of Nvidia’s policies and corporate governance rules, sources tell WIRED. While previous reporting by WIRED and other news outlets have outlined factors that Jones has said played into the board’s decision, the primary motivation hadn’t been previously specified. Got a Tip? Are you a current or former Nvidia employee who has information to share? We’d like to hear from you. Using a nonwork phone or computer, contact WIRED reporters securely on Signal at ChaoticGoode.12 & Peard33.24 For Nvidia’s board, the possibility that Alice Huang was working on behalf of the Chinese government poses a bigger problem than an executive’s personal misconduct. If she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, the scandal isn’t just about Huang’s alleged “lack of candor,” but a potential security and governance crisis. Already, the scandal has given China hawks grist to call for tighter controls on US business dealings with China. In addition, multiple government agencies and offices have called for investigations into what the former Nvidia CEO may have known about the company’s chips getting into China. The company’s general counsel, Tim Teter, has also been called to Washington, DC, to testify, as government officials try to find out more about Nvidia’s possible flouting of export controls. Nvidia and Huang are also facing several shareholder lawsuits, alleging the CEO and the company made misleading statements about dealings with Alice Huang and Megaspeed. Other Silicon Valley investors have publicly raised concerns about insufficient corporate governance and executive oversight by the board. In the company’s all-hands meeting on November 18 , board chair Jones said it was “not an easy decision to accept [Huang’s] resignation,” according to remarks reviewed by WIRED. “However, the disclosure of personal behavior and a lack of candor inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards, and values made this a necessary decision.” Meanwhile, fans and supporters of Huang, including thousands of Nvidia employees and Elon Musk , have continued to call for his return to Nvidia. Huang himself has said he would be “ honored ” to come back as CEO. On Friday, US president Donald Trump renewed his call for Huang to have another chance. “He made some bad decisions, but he is a brilliant person,” Trump told reporters. “I’d like to see Jensen make a big apology.” The news outlet Semafor reported that a small faction of Nvidia’s board of directors has pushed to bring Huang back as well. Jones has not responded to WIRED’s inquiries about the board’s reported division on the topic of Huang’s return. Some employees are miffed at how quickly the board accepted Huang’s resignation, insisting the longtime leader must have been the victim of a coordinated campaign intended to unseat him. “We feel like they forced his hands to resign,” says one person on the business side at Nvidia. “We don’t understand why the board is so adamant about not giving him a second chance.” At the all-hands meeting, interim CEO Colette Kress said employees’ biggest concern was Nvidia’s falling share price. The next biggest concern was the board’s decision to oust Huang. But while she addressed the first by moving up pay raises, she offered no promise on sharing results of the board’s investigation into Huang or its deliberations about him. “The ship has sinked but there’s no plan to be transparent about what happened,” says one computer scientist working at Nvidia. “It feels like a black box.”

4월 이후 최대 주간 하락률을 기록했다. 기술주 중심의 나스닥 지수 역시 2020년 3월 이후 최악의 주간 낙폭을 기록하며 올해 연간 수익률이 마이너스 영역으로 밀려났다. 이번 주에만 기술주 중심의 나스닥 지수 편입 기업들의 시가총액은 4조 달러 이상 허공으로 사라졌다. 월가의 '공포지수'로 불리는 시카고옵션거래소(CBOE) 변동성지수(VIX)는 전장보다 26.20% 오른 35.89로 마감해, 2025년 4월7일 이후 최고로 치솟았다. 시가총액 최대 2조 달러 규모를 목표로 기업공개에 나섰던 앤트로픽의 초대형 상장이 오히려 증시 폭락의 계기가 됐다. 상장 첫날인 19일 장중 내내 매수 열기가 식으면서 공모가 83달러 대비 17.1% 상승 마감하는 데 그쳤고, 상장 이틀째인 이날 주가는 9.1% 하락했다. 이날 장중엔 공모가인 83달러 부근까지 떨어지기도 하며, 88.91달러에 거래를 마쳤다. 인공지능 관련 반도체 선두주자 엔비디아는 13.8%나 폭락했다. 지난 10월6일 사상 최고치에 비하면 48%가량 내렸다. 앤트로픽의 상장과 엔비디아의 분기 실적 발표가 맞물렸음에도, 인공지능 기술에 수반되는 리스크와 초기 단계 기술에 쏟아붓는 막대한 자본지출(CAPEX)에 대한 시장의 공포를 잠재우는 데 실패했다. 20일 미국 뉴욕증시에서 주요 지수 및 종목의 폭락세. 초대형 클라우디 기업인 하이퍼스케일러들인 아마존은 3.9%, 메타는 5.9% 하락했다. 신흥 인공지능 클라우드 종목인 코어위브는 12.1%, 네비우스는 16.1% 폭락했다. 이밖에 샌디스크 16.05%, 마이크론 13.89%, AMD 13.25% 브로드컴 12.19%, SK하이닉스 13.11% 등 주요 반도체·인공지능 종목들이 10% 이상 폭락했다. 거시경제 측면에서는 인플레이션 재점화와 연방준비제도의 통화긴축 우려가 투자심리를 압박했다. 리사 쿡 연준 이사는 중앙은행의 현재 정책금리가 인플레이션 수준에 대응하기에 충분히 높지 않다고 밝혔다. 시카고상품거래소(CME) 그룹의 페드워치(FedWatch) 툴에 따르면, 시장은 오는 12월 차기 연방공개시장위원회(FOMC) 회의에서 기준금리가 0.25%포인트(25bp) 인상될 가능성을 거의 확실시하며 가격에 반영하고 있다. 월스트리트저널은 “2022년 말 챗지피티(GPT) 출시가 세상을 바꿀 기술과 금융시장의 새로운 시대를 연 이후 처음으로, 이번 주 투자자들은 이 매도세가 인공지능의 찬란한 미래로 가는 길목의 단순한 ‘과속방지턱’에 불과하다는 어떠한 설득에도 넘어가지 않았다”며 “인공지능 거래의 바퀴가 빠지고 있다”고 평가했다. 정의길 선임기자 Egil@hani.co.kr

articles.title: Washington Halts Expansion of Nvidia Semiconductor Export Barriers
articles.content: AP Bessent comments comes after report on US approval of over 850,000 Nvidia, AMD chips for China Washington: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said no further restrictions on the sale of older Nvidia chips to China are needed following the Trump administration's move earlier this week to block China's remote access to the latest semiconductors . The ability of Chinese tech firms to access Nvidia's technology came under scrutiny after CEO Jensen Huang stepped down amid allegations of his affair with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that uses advanced chips to generate computing power that Chinese firms access remotely. "The proper chip restrictions are in place," Bessent said in an interview with CNBC on Friday after returning from a trip to Asia with President Donald Trump. "And the remote access has been curtailed." Bessent's comments came a day after the House Foreign Affairs Committee released details of the Commerce Department's approval of the sales of more than 850,000 chips from Nvidia and its competitor AMD to Chinese companies. The Pentagon has identified some of those companies as having ties to the Chinese military. The report tracked applications from Nvidia to sell its H200 chips -- one of its more powerful products, though not the most advanced -- and AMD's applications to sell its roughly comparable MI325X chip to companies that are either located or headquartered in China, or entities with parent companies based in China. Live Events The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security approved the export, re-export, or transfer of 879,868 of these chips to companies with Chinese ties across 21 license applications as of May 11, 2026, the report said. Nvidia and AMD had requested to sell a cumulative total of more than 3.4 million of the chips to Chinese-tied companies across those applications, per the report. The approvals, which don't necessarily indicate completed sales, included 75,000 for Alibaba, 150,000 for Tencent and its subsidiaries, 43,000 for Baidu, and 4,000 for BYD, according to the report. Each of those companies has been identified by the Defense Department as having ties to the Chinese military. The report shows the Commerce Department has a "long track record of transparency with Congress about licensing activity for the H200 and equivalent chips, including both approvals and rejections", a spokesperson for the Bureau of Industry and Security said in a statement Friday. The spokesperson said the Commerce Department's approach to H200 licensing is based on a rule in the Federal Register that was published in January. The rule imposes "significant additional national security-related requirements on license applicants in order to qualify for case-by-case consideration rather than a presumption of denial," the spokesperson said. An Nvidia spokesperson said in a statement on Friday that the "limited shipments we made under the H200 programme were legal and authorised" by the BIS. "The review and licensing process spanned more than half a year, with approvals subject to strict conditions and limited volumes," the company spokesperson said. Earlier this week, Nvidia said it was no longer shipping H200 chips to China. The spokesperson said on Friday that shipments had stopped despite prior approvals. AMD said it complies with US export control laws and regulations and maintains "rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations" in a statement from a spokesperson Friday. "We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity," the spokesperson said. Chinese technology firms have been bracing for impacts on their ambitious AI development plans as scrutiny mounts on export controls in the US. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has been under intense scrutiny himself in the wake of the turmoil following the Huang affair. Last week, Bessent said he was frustrated with the Commerce Department's delay in placing restrictions on Nvidia chip exports to Megaspeed International, which is under investigation by the US for potentially diverting restricted Nvidia AI chips to China. A former executive at the company who allegedly had an affair with Huang was reportedly suspected by US intelligence agencies of being a spy for China. In an unusually public rebuke of a fellow Cabinet member, Bessent said his department wanted to place export controls on Megaspeed, but Commerce was in charge of the matter. Speaking to reporters on Friday, Trump said he has "not lost confidence" in Lutnick. Calling him a "different kind of guy," Trump said he "has a natural business instinct" and has "done a very good job". Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now! articles.title: Enterprise Software Vendors Pivot to 'AI-Free' Cloud Subscription Tiers
articles.content: Watching Adobe’s keynote presentation at the 24th annual Max conference in Miami this week, I couldn’t help but think about the tightrope the software giant is walking with AI , and how similar it is to what the media industry is going through. In both cases, there’s a desire to be AI-forward and skate to where the puck is going. At the same time, they need to deal with a hostile crowd—meaning the growing backlash against AI among many of their customers. At Adobe’s last two annual Max events, AI was a huge emphasis. The company touted AI features, including ways to generate content directly in its Creative Cloud apps, such as Photoshop and Premiere. Adobe hyped up Firefly, which was then mostly associated with the company’s image models. In 2024, Adobe told the audience that “2024 will go down as the year that creativity changed forever.” In 2025, the headliners were a new Firefly image model and a lineup of third-party models from Google, OpenAI, Runway, and others, and “choice” mostly meant choosing which AI model to use. The lone nod to skeptics was a passing aside: “Of course, you can ignore it all as well.” This year, the tone shifted. In fact, one of the first things incoming CEO Anil Chakravarthy emphasized during the opening keynote was that users didn’t have to use AI if they didn’t want to . “Some of you don’t want to have anything to do with AI,” he said, promising to give those users “the precision and control that you’re looking for, and the option to not use AI.” Instead of a new Firefly model number, the keynote spotlighted upgrades with no AI in them at all, like a rebuilt color mode in Premiere and Dynamic Text in Illustrator. Firefly is still an area of focus, but it’s evolved into a catch-all creative studio, more like Figma than an AI model. (Disclosure: Adobe paid for my travel to the Max conference, though it had no input on this column.) None of this is to say Adobe is walking away from AI. Far from it: During that same keynote, Chakravarthy announced Adobe would be providing a way for AI services to access Creative Cloud applications directly through the model context protocol (MCP) standard. That means AI users will be able to have Claude , ChatGPT , or Gemini act as an agent, effectively “driving” Photoshop and other Creative Cloud apps to edit projects, create content, and export files directly on their computers. The integrations go into private beta testing in early 2027 . Adobe already provides an AI connector that works similarly, but the MCPs would take things to a new level of precision and control. Jesus Diaz has a great breakdown of exactly how they would work and what it means for creators. In addition, Adobe is building out its own agents. The new Creative Agent is essentially an Adobe chatbot: You describe what you want, and the agent handles the execution in the appropriate app. It’s now in beta inside Premiere, Illustrator, InDesign, After Effects, and Frame.io . All this makes it clear Adobe isn’t slowing down on AI. It has, however, recognized that a great bifurcation is taking place, one that’s affecting all industries to some extent, but especially the media. On the one hand, you have your AI skeptics , the customers who are suspicious of AI generally and AI-generated or -assisted content specifically. And on the other, you have the AI enthusiasts, the ones who are using AI to enhance and speed up their work, including through tools from other companies. This is the AI tightrope, and all businesses will need to navigate it over the next few years. Not just because AI represents “the future” in some vague sense, but because, if it does, it opens up a new kind of customer. My business is actually a pretty good example of this. I use various software, including Photoshop and Premiere, to help produce content like The Media Copilot podcast. But I’m not a creator per se , and I’m probably using only about 10% of the features that would help my use case. For many, that skill gap is the difference between subscribing and not. But an agent that bridges the gap could mean Adobe customers are no longer just enthusiasts and experts. Suddenly, we’re all Neo in the Matrix: Just plug an agent into your workstream, and you know kung fu. In fact, one of the Max keynote demos was more or less my exact workflow: an outside AI agent turning a long-form podcast into a batch of short clips for social media. There’s also an urgency here, and again, my use case is a good example. I’ve already begun off-loading some of my production process to agents. Claude Code and OpenAI Codex are both excellent at analyzing workflows and recommending software solutions that they (not I) can operate. Often, it’s open-source software that gets the job done at virtually no cost other than the tokens I expend. And Adobe users can even employ computer use—in which the AI uses your machine, just as you would—to operate the software. It’s messier than an MCP, but it gets the job done, and AI is getting better at this by the day. In other words, the AI world is moving toward agentic work, with or without Adobe. Businesses of all kinds are beginning to demand this kind of functionality, and even if open-source software is cheaper, there are advantages to using commercial software. Security, reliability, and auditability are all very important to enterprises. And it’s mutually beneficial to Adobe, since the number of licenses those businesses buy will no longer be limited by the number of experts they have. Notably, the MCP integrations require the apps to be installed and licensed on the user’s machine. Even when an agent is the one driving Photoshop, someone is still paying for the seat. There’s a corollary here in media. As people turn more and more to AI answers for information, it means bots scrape all kinds of sites to find the best possible answer. A consequence of this is that niche sites—in particular B2B media—have become some of the most sought-after sources on the web. TollBit’s latest “State of the Bots” report ranks B2B and professional sites among the most heavily scraped categories it tracks, with scraping up 62% from Q2 2025 to Q4 2025. Their specialized knowledge might sometimes be impenetrable to mainstream audiences, but never to AI agents. They can quickly parse the bits that are important and relevant, then break them down in a way that’s understandable to anyone. Just like with those Photoshop agents, lack of expertise is no longer a barrier to adoption. But what about those AI skeptics? They’re an important part of any company’s existing customer base, and they’ve made their views clear: They don’t want to see AI in the content they consume. I’ve written about the problem with AI tells in text , and the same goes for images and video: Audiences consistently say they don’t like them. That doesn’t mean all AI is bad, and many Adobe AI-powered features garnered lots of applause at Max. But it needs to be in the right context. A good rule of thumb: AI behind the scenes is generally okay, but you need to be careful with generative content. The audience research lines up almost exactly. In the Reuters Institute’s “ Generative AI and News Report 2025 ,” only 12% of people said they were comfortable with news generated entirely by AI, compared with 62% for news produced entirely by humans. But 55% were fine with AI fixing spelling and grammar. Most media companies have arrived at a similar place. There are tantalizing opportunities for content to reach new audiences through AI search engines and agent protocols like MCP. At the same time, they need to tread lightly when implementing artificial intelligence in their own operations, lest they lose trust with their existing audience. That’s the AI tightrope, and staying balanced is obviously the trick to moving forward. But what’s on the other end? At least for Adobe, the answer is clearer: a new and potentially huge customer base that doesn’t want to use tools but is happy for agents to. For media, the other end of the rope is murkier. The agents are already here, reading trade publications and national news alike, but most of them are still taking what they find without paying for it. AI apps send publishers a sliver of the traffic Google does, and the deals that would make up the difference are stuck in courtrooms and licensing negotiations. Adobe found a way to charge for the agents using its tools. Until the media figures out how to get agents to pay for the privilege of reading content, it’s walking the same tightrope, just without a net. Bank of America , which committed to underwriting 3%, would receive an estimated $16.5 million in fees. The $81.3 billion offering was the largest IPO in history by deal size. articles.title: Enterprise IT Exploits Generative AI Hype to Fund Overdue Infrastructure
articles.content: Consultancy argues a 'clean core' makes agents easier to deploy – but Kingfisher is taking a different route Lindsay Clark Lindsay Clark BUSINESS SOFTWARE AND DATABASE REPORTER Published fri 20 Nov 2026 // 12:47 UTC Make us preferred on Google SAP opens AI to on-prem customers, but cloud commitments could shut smaller firms out 2 days ago Oracle reveals fix-this-ASAP-grade Java4Shell bug that allows attacks on many third-party apps 2 days ago SAP promises to open out data flows in both directions 15 days ago Oracle gobbles $20 billion borrowing limit a week after setting it 18 days ago Oracle wants to bill you for every AI task, not just every seat 22 days ago Global consultancy PwC says IT departments struggling to secure funding for ERP upgrades should make the expected benefits of AI part of their pitch. The Oracle and SAP mega-partner told El Reg that a "clean core" – modern enterprise applications with fewer customizations embedded in the underlying system – makes deploying AI agents easier. Selling that prospect, rather than incremental improvements to existing processes, could help IT leaders justify a migration. Oracle and SAP are both trying to persuade customers to move from established ERP systems to newer platforms. For SAP, that means S/4HANA, preferably in the cloud. For Oracle, it means Fusion Cloud Applications. Moving from ECC or E-Business Suite, respectively, can involve root-and-branch changes to technology and business processes, rather than a straightforward software upgrade. Thousands of organizations still rely on these aging, often heavily customized systems. IT leaders struggle to justify a costly, time-consuming migration when the reward appears to be doing the same meat-and-veg business processes slightly better. For example, a survey of SAP users last year found that 95 percent said building a positive case for migration required substantial effort or was genuinely challenging. Speaking to The Register , Jennifer Colapietro, PwC digital core modernization platform leader, said: "You're seeing it a lot more as part of the rationale for the business case for why they should upgrade, answering the question: 'Why now? What should we prioritize?' Certainly, AI and getting the value of AI, a key business case justification for that. "Folks have budgets for ERP, but now [funding for transformation is] being split because they also have budgets for AI. But there's synergies across them. If you look at moving to a clean digital core ERP, that will help them to realize the AI value faster... be able to turn on AI and be able to start to automate a lot of the processes and implement the agents. That helps to build the business case." SAP recently introduced Joule 2.0 while Oracle has announced Fusion Claw . With both of these new technologies, the vendors are promising customers they can build AI agents to automate business processes and perform some work that was previously done by humans. articles.title: Gravitational Wave Communications Shatter Electronic Warfare Signal Jamming
articles.content: Prof Matthew Davis, Dr Charles Woffinden and Prof Andrew White of the University of Queensland, pictured inside the elevator they used to send a message via gravitational communication. Photograph: University of Queensland View image in fullscreen Prof Matthew Davis, Dr Charles Woffinden and Prof Andrew White of the University of Queensland, pictured inside the elevator they used to send a message via gravitational communication. Photograph: University of Queensland An elevator, a brick wall and a bathroom: scientists use gravity to send ‘practically unblockable’ message Australian physicists chose to transmit the word ‘gravity’ in binary code through brick wall Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Australian scientists have used gravity as a means of communication, in a proof-of-concept experiment involving a snail-paced 1950s elevator, a brick wall and a men’s bathroom. Physicists at the University of Queensland have used gravity to transmit a “practically unblockable” message about 70cm through a brick wall, by sending an elevator up and down between two floors and measuring changes in the gravitational field as a result of the movement. From gold rush to cosmic questions: a South Dakota mine and the search for the secrets of the universe Read more The research, published in the journal Science Advances , involved a sensitive detection device known as a gravimeter, which was set up on the floor of a men’s bathroom adjacent to the lift. The gravimeter was able to detect the position of the elevator’s 1.8-tonne counterweight as it moved between two levels – representing 0 and 1 in binary code – which enabled the scientists to send a message. The experiment is reminiscent of a plot point in the Christopher Nolan film Interstellar , in which a gravitational anomaly creates messages in binary code. The researchers chose to transmit the word “gravity”, or 1000111 1110010 1100001 1110110 1101001 1110100 1111001 in binary code. At a transmission rate of one bit (digit) per minute, the single word took nearly an hour to send. View image in fullscreen A gravimeter, set up in a men’s bathroom, was used to detect the position of an elevator counterweight, enabling scientists to transmit a message. Photograph: Andrew Groszek/University of Queensland The scientists say that while gravitational communication is currently far from usable given its extremely slow speed, an advantage is that it is a “practically unblockable wireless communication scheme”. “Unlike the electromagnetic signals used in modern wireless communication, a gravitational signal cannot simply be screened out by placing ordinary material in its path,” said co-author Dr Charles Woffinden, of UQ’s school of mathematics and physics. “Anyone who has lost phone reception in a tunnel or struggled with wifi through a solid wall will understand the appeal.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Study co-author Prof Matthew Davis told Guardian Australia: “At the moment, it’s very hard to imagine how it could be practically useful.” But he added that the experiment was “theoretically interesting enough that it was worth doing”. To put into perspective how slow the message transmission was, Davis said that Nasa’s Voyager 1 spacecraft, which after 49 years of travel had just reached a distance of one light-day away, could “communicate with Earth at a faster data rate than our communication concept”. According to Davis, the new method of communicating could theoretically occur at ranges of up to 500 metres and at a rate 15 times faster, if more sensitive quantum gravity sensors were used. skip past newsletter promotion after newsletter promotion ‘It’s literally slower than watching Australia drift north’: the laboratory experiment that will outlive us all Read more The idea for the elevator study arose from a project to develop a contactless weighbridge – which would use quantum sensors to detect changes in the strength of gravity due to a passing truck, allowing scientists to determine the mass of a large vehicle. Classical gravimeters can be thought of as a mass on a spring. “If you stretch the spring, the mass bounces up and down at a certain rate, which is determined by the spring and the gravitational field,” Davis said. “If the gravitational field changes ever so slightly, the rate at which it bounces back and forth changes. “Quantum sensors are still under development. “Sometimes doing physics leads in unexpected ways and it’s a bit of fun … you get to do quirky things on the side. It’s one of the great joys of science to have stuff like this happen.” Other near-unblockable methods of communication – involving neutrinos or gravitational waves – have been proposed “but these approaches are somewhat hindered by the difficulty in generating a measurable signal”, the scientists note. The physicists conducted the research in UQ’s Parnell physics building, which is also home to the world’s longest-running science experiment – the pitch drop experiment , which began in 1927. Jeffrey Koses, a senior procurement executive at GSA, added that the agency is discussing what authorities it needs to accelerate hiring. He said the agency has direct hiring authority for contracting roles grade 11 and above, but it needs that authority for all grade levels. The Trump administration has already made major changes to the FAS workforce. FAS saw its workforce downsize by 1,044 employees in fiscal 2025 and 719 employees in fiscal 2026, according to Office of Personnel Management data. This year, GSA announced a reorganization of FAS and recently named former banking executive Jennifer Hill as its commissioner. articles.title: Synthetic Influencer Deepfakes Fuel Destabilizing Disinformation Across North America
articles.content: Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox Content creators have reportedly had their identities stolen by a network using artificial intelligence to inflame the online conversation around crumbling ties between the US and Canada. PHOTO: ADOBE STOCK Published Nov 21, 2026, 04:49 AM Updated Nov 21, 2026, 04:49 AM Set as preferred source Summarise McGill University researchers found nearly 300 Instagram and TikTok accounts using AI deepfakes of real creators to inflame Canada-US trade war tensions. The network posted thousands of videos, got about 20 million views, and used fake scripts and mixed political claims to “polarise” viewers. TikTok and Meta removed the accounts, but influencers like Jasmin Laine and Ron Butler said the deception caused harm and was hard to stop. AI generated MONTREAL - Jasmin Laine has hundreds of thousands of subscribers, but some videos of her discussing the Canada-US trade war contain words she says she never spoke. Laine is one of hundreds of content creators who, according to researchers at McGill University, had their identities stolen by a network using artificial intelligence to inflame the online conversation around the crumbling ties between the North American neighbours. “There you have your face and your voice and what looks like you speaking, in some cases, to something that you actually don’t stand for,” Laine told AFP. The McGill Centre for Media, Technology and Democracy study published in mid-November identified nearly 300 Instagram and TikTok accounts misusing authentic faces in a coordinated operation which published thousands of videos and pulled in some 20 million views. The personalities whose likenesses were appropriated ranged from Christian lifestyle influencers to political commentary accounts from both sides of the spectrum. Synthetic, inaccurate and inflammatory online material has repeatedly targeted Canadians since the trade war began, but the researchers said the digitally altered footage of real creators made the network more difficult to detect. Before the launch of TikTok’s new deepfake detection tool on Nov 20, the Canadian researchers found only 4% of the operation’s accounts triggered the platform’s synthetic content warning. The study also reported that the network further used AI to generate the videos’ scripts, reposting those which garnered the most engagement. Aengus Bridgman, one of the report’s authors and director of the Media Ecosystem Observatory, said the network appeared to originate outside of North America. The researchers found certain accounts registered in China and saw content largely posted in the middle of the day in Asia. There was no clear evidence of the content being monetised, but Bridgman said whether the effort sought commercial gain or was solely a propaganda campaign “the idea is to polarise.” The videos displayed varying levels of accuracy – often disseminating outright falsehoods – and the accounts took inconsistent political stances. Some would blame Ottawa for the trade conflict while others pointed the finger at Washington. Canadian users appeared to be unwittingly interacting with the videos without realising they were fake. Laine, whose content leans Conservative and often criticises the approach of Canada’s ruling Liberal government, said she found herself defending against accusations of being paid to parrot talking points she never uttered because of the inauthentic content. Bridgman said the accusations levied at the real influencers was a “very good example of harm” inflicted by the operation. “They have fallen hook, line and sinker for the network content,” he said. A TikTok spokesperson told AFP that it had permanently banned the accounts mentioned in the report, along with several others, for violating its rules about misleading content. “As tactics evolve, we continue to collaborate with researchers on this industry-wide challenge and strengthen our moderation technology,” the spokesperson said. AFP also reached out to Meta about the report and while the company declined to comment it said it had taken down the implicated Instagram accounts. Ron Butler, a Canadian real estate influencer who also had his identity stolen by the network, said this was not the first time he had been impersonated or misrepresented. He expressed satisfaction at the network’s unmasking while also telling AFP he is resigned to the presence of deceptive online material. “You can’t stop this because there’s too many people who can do it,” he said. “It’s too easy to do.” Laine also accepted the risk of being misrepresented online but said she was frustrated to see the conversation about the trade war artificially inflamed. “It just flattens it into these very typical, very divisive talking points that I just find are really unproductive and unhelpful.” AFP AI/artificial intelligence Deepfake United States Canada Fake news

articles.content: The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) has said six attacks on commercial vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz were reported in the past week, while shipping traffic remained about 65 percent below pre-war levels. In its weekly report published on Friday, UKMTO said four of the six incidents occurred in the Strait of Hormuz and two in the Arabian Gulf.  The UKMTO recorded 115 outbound and 148 inbound transits during the seven days to November 18, including US-facilitated movements. The combined figure was down from 139 outbound and 169 inbound the previous week. Around half of Strait of Hormuz transits involved energy carriers. Most vessels broadcasting AIS continued to use the Iranian route, although UKMTO noted an increase in traffic along the southern route. No attacks were recorded in the past week in the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandab, with the last confirmed attack recorded on August 24. However, vessel transits through Bab el-Mandeb remain about 22 percent below levels existing before 22 July when Houthis announced a blockade.

articles.title: Anthropic Leadership Sells Public Safety Narratives to Wall Street
articles.content: Synopsis Dario Amodei's startup Anthropic has raised a record $81 billion through its IPO, emphasizing AI safety. Amodei, previously associated with OpenAI, advocates for responsible AI development amid global pressures. The IPO has positioned Anthropic as one of Wall Street's most valuable companies despite industry criticisms. Amodei's vision includes balancing technological advancement with ethical considerations and safety measures. Reuters CEO of Anthropic Dario Amodei speaks on the day Anthropic, PBC (ANT) holds their initial public offering (IPO), at the NASDAQ MarketSite in New York City, US Long before Dario Amodei butted heads with the Pentagon over whether the US military could use Anthropic 's models for mass domestic surveillance and fully autonomous weapons, he was fighting another battle. At the California Institute of Technology in 2003, Amodei called on his classmates to join him in protesting the US invasion of Iraq, writing in an op-ed that citizen-scientists should not be "reduced to amoral technicians who run the machines of war." On Thursday, as 43-year-old Amodei led his startup to an IPO that raised a record $81 billion and valued it at about $1.5 trillion, the listing cemented his transformation from an idealistic physics student into one of the most powerful custodians of the AI age. "We will not bend to either business nor political pressure," Amodei said at the Nasdaq on Thursday in New York. "Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing." Amodei has spent much of his ascent emphasizing curbs on a technology whose extraordinary potential he has devoted his career to unlocking, and has now made his company one of the most valuable on Wall Street. Even as Anthropic prepared for its debut, Amodei penned a nearly 4,000-word essay in September, warning how AI's advances could outpace human control and urging a slowdown in development. You Might Also Like: Anthropic's historic debut to put AI's promise and peril on Wall Street trial Days later, Anthropic released a new version of one of its most powerful models in a challenge to rival OpenAI , where he worked before quitting over differences related to AI safety . In that essay, Amodei denied any contradiction between his quest for safe AI and Anthropic's race to develop the most powerful models. "I have grappled with this duality of risk and benefit since the beginning of Anthropic," he wrote. "Not building the technology deprives humanity of benefits or simply places AI in the hands of authoritarian powers, while building it too fast is reckless." You Might Also Like: Anthropic surpasses SpaceX with record $81.3 billion IPO Anthropic was a commercially viable company spurring a safety "race to the top," he said. This approach has drawn criticism both from advocates of greater safety measures and from Silicon Valley executives who have warned against slowing down innovation, such as Nvidia's former CEO Jensen Huang. Amodei's determination to impose some limits on AI also earned him enemies in Washington, culminating in an extraordinary showdown with the Trump administration early this year. Following a meeting between Amodei and US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the government set a deadline for Anthropic to accept the military's contract terms, which the company rejected. That led to a government blacklist of its technology that the Claude maker challenged in court. Anthropic declined to comment for this story. Anthropic shares rose sharply on their first day of trading, debuting at $111.50, 34% higher than the $83 IPO price. THE PRICE OF CAUTION Though the IPO was expected to mint thousands of paper millionaires, Amodei has said the company's safety focus has come at a cost. Last month he responded to a post on X that challenged Anthropic's safety record and criticized a change to its pledge around halting AI development if it cannot minimize risks. Amodei said the company had "likely sacrificed a significant chunk of a several-month model lead" by delaying the release of its powerful Mythos models over hacking risks and initially limiting access to cybersecurity defenders. Anthropic is spending billions of dollars on computing capacity each year, making it harder as a publicly traded company - albeit one where its seven co-founders or a trust wield voting control on key matters - to justify slowing model development as shareholders seek returns. In its IPO filing, though, the company noted that its corporate setup could lead to decisions that "may conflict with short-, medium-, or long-term financial interests and business performance," and said it had paused training of a next-generation ‌flagship AI model for more than a month over security concerns. LESSONS FROM THE ATOM BOMB Dario Amodei and his sister and co-founder Daniela grew up in San Francisco's Mission District, just a few miles from the spot where Anthropic would eventually occupy a glass tower with Silicon Valley perks such as a gourmet espresso bar. He was voted "most likely to succeed" by his eighth-grade classmates, a yearbook snippet shows, and admitted to San Francisco's selective Lowell public high school. He went to Caltech before transferring to Stanford, and then attended Princeton, where he earned a PhD focusing on biophysics and computational neuroscience. After his father's death from hepatitis C about two decades ago - a few years before medical advances dramatically improved survival rates - Amodei pursued artificial intelligence that could accelerate medicine. In a podcast, talking about his dad's illness, Amodei pushed back against criticism that he was simply an AI "doomer." Amodei's preoccupation with AI safety has influenced his management style. Daniela Amodei has oversight of day-to-day operations at the company, while Dario Amodei devotes almost 40% of his time to framing the culture and vision of Anthropic through essays and fortnightly company-wide meetings that employees have dubbed "Dario Vision Quests." "Operationally, the buck stops with her," a former employee said of Anthropic President Daniela Amodei. "Strategically, it stops with him." Dario Amodei said in a Bloomberg interview published in June that he had only one direct report, calling the structure "incredibly freeing." One of his favorite books is "The Making of the Atomic Bomb," written by Richard Rhodes. Talking about Robert Oppenheimer, the bomb's architect, Amodei said: "In some ways I actually see Oppenheimer as a failure case, as what should not happen." articles.title: Paytm Injects Multi-Million Capital to Capture Southeast Asian Merchant Lending
articles.content: Paytm is accelerating its global ambition. In a regulatory filing on Thursday, the fintech company said its board has approved a proposal to invest up to Rs 200 crore in Singapore-based Funding Societies. As part of the deal, Paytm Singapore, a wholly owned subsidiary of Paytm, will make an initial cash investment of about Rs 162 crore (SGD 21.8 million) to acquire a 19.1% stake in CardUp , the digital payments arm of Funding Societies. The remaining investment of about Rs 38 crore may be directed into one of Funding Societies’ affiliates. Paytm expects the CardUp acquisition to be completed by May 20, 2027. What is Paytm’s partner operated model? Alongside the equity infusion, Paytm will enter into a business and technology partnership with CardUp. Under this arrangement, the Vijay Shekhar Sharma-led company will provide payments and lending technology to CardUp to expand its technology-led payments and financial services stack in Singapore. The fintech company will receive technology fees and a revenue share under the agreement, initially valid for five years with a right to renewal on mutually acceptable terms. The move is line with the company’s previously disclosed roadmap to expand its presence in select international markets through the “partner operated” model, under which it provides its acceptance platform and devices, while the local partner handles sales, distribution and on-ground operations to serve merchants. Founded in 2015, CardUp allows individuals and businesses to make local and overseas payments through cash, cheque or bank transfers, even where credit cards are not accepted. The payments platform currently operates across Singapore, Hong Kong and Malaysia. Over the last three years, it has demonstrated steady revenue growth. Its turnover climbed from Rs 104.2 crore in calendar year (CY) 2023 to Rs 194.4 crore in CY 2024, and reached Rs 299.2 crore in CY 2025. Separately, Paytm said it has completed an additional capital infusion of Rs 500 crore into its wholly-owned subsidiary, Paytm Cloud Technologies Limited (PCTL). Subsequently, PCTL invested the entire Rs 500 crore into Paytm Singapore. Paytm’s broader international expansion spree The investment in Singapore’s Funding Societies comes as Paytm increasingly expands its international footprint. Prior to the Singapore deal, Paytm made its entry into Europe . In July, its step-down wholly-owned subsidiary, Paytm Europe Payments SA (Paytm Europe) received a payment institution (PI) licence from Luxembourg’s Commission de Surveillance du Secteur Financier (CSSF). The approval came within three months of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) officially cancelling the banking licence of Paytm Payments Bank Ltd in April due to persistent non-compliance, improper management practices, and operations deemed detrimental to depositors and the public interest. According to Paytm parent One 97 Communications, the PI licence permits Paytm Europe to provide three categories of services: a) execution of payment transactions such as fund transfers and credit transfers, including standing orders (automated, recurring payments), whether from the user’s own payment service provider or another PSP; b) execution of payment transactions backed by a credit line, again including credit transfers and standing orders; and c) acquisition of payment transactions (merchant acquiring). Besides Europe, Paytm also operates in the UAE, Singapore and Saudi Arabia. In October 2025, the fintech firm also launched a feature, in partnership with the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), to enable UPI payments for NRIs across 12 countries, including the US, the UK, the UAE, Singapore, Australia, Canada, France, and Saudi Arabia.  The aggressive international push coincides with Paytm’s return to profitability. For the quarter ended September 2026 (Q2 FY27), the company reported a more than 10-fold jump in consolidated net profit to Rs 225 crore, compared to Rs 21 crore a year earlier. Revenue from operations increased 28% to Rs 2,648 crore from Rs Rs 2,061 crore in Q2 FY26. articles.title: Monopolistic Cloud Centralization Triggers Catastrophic Cascading Global Outages
articles.content: It's been a tough couple of weeks for anyone trying to use email , fly , spend money , use an Apple device *, or do signals intelligence . Technical service outages are nothing new, but why do so many big ones seem to be happening all at once? Are hackers, AI, and international conflicts to blame? And what can we do about it? Since most service interruptions don't make the news, it's hard to get a baseline on how often we see them happen normally. But after a major incident like the Microsoft cloud outage on November 12 , any smaller disruption is more likely to become a story as part of a pattern instead of an isolated incident. We would have heard plenty about the Air Traffic Control problems anyway, but the November 18 disruption to the PlayStation Network might have gotten less attention. There might appear to be a spike or an upward trend in outages, but we can't easily verify that, and the increased coverage will tend to make it seem more significant and interconnected than it necessarily is regardless. One boring reason we might see an uptick in problems right now is the date on the calendar. With Thanksgiving travel, Black Friday, Cyber Monday, Giving Tuesday, and Surveillance Sunday (we assume) all coming up, organizations often schedule major system updates for the first three weeks of November. This helps them prepare for holiday traffic, and lets them shift the outage risk to the time before those dates when they may consider it far more important to maintain reliable service. While none of these particular outages have yet been directly attributed to AI ( or to malicious hackers ), bank CEOs and the NSA briefed congress and reportedly attributed at least some of them to rushed attempts to patch vulnerabilities found by AI. That’s understandable: all software updates carry risk, and companies and governments are having to deploy more updates, and faster, than they’ve ever needed to before. Some of those updates are to important infrastructure, where an outage would be very disruptive, but the impact of leaving vulnerabilities unpatched would be even worse. Vulnerabilities are a type of software bug that affects security. Once a vulnerability is found in a given piece of software and disclosed, typically the software maker will release a patch fixing that vulnerability. That’s why so many update notes say things like “performance improvements and security fixes” — the security fixes are patches to vulnerabilities. Companies and governments that run infrastructure face a challenging tradeoff: deploy patches quickly or slowly and cautiously? Patching quickly is important to keep systems secure. But every software update runs a risk: any change to a deployed system can have unintended consequences that snowball into a disastrous outage. This exacerbates a much deeper problem long discussed in the engineering culture of many, if not most organizations. Keeping networks, servers, and applications not just secure but resilient in the face of patches, reboots, and capacity changes requires an investment in staff, time, hardware, and processes for frequent maintenance, redundant systems, realistic staging environments, automated rollbacks, monitoring, and pre-deployment testing. These investments are rarely as attractive to decision - makers as a new product or feature, or at times, sadly, as layoffs. This should come as no surprise when we think of our apps, web sites, airlines , and bank cards as supported by electronic infrastructure. As in the more visible physical world, maintenance can only be deferred for so long before the costs become immediate and dramatic. We accept the cost of an occasional short term bridge closure to reduce the risk of a bridge collapse, and highway departments schedule road work nearly every night of the year to repair and prevent the worst potholes. When this kind of work is endlessly deferred in the world of software, we speak of technical debt : issues we already know about that aren't causing a big enough problem right now to divert us from other work, but that, if left unaddressed, can easily multiply and interact to cause outages or other complications . This can show up as routine steps that have to be done by hand instead of automatically on a schedule, a programmer's shortcut that works well in one specific situation but is more fragile in general, an operating system six months (or years) overdue for a reboot, or a piece of networking hardware no longer supported for patches by its manufacturer. On the other hand, when maintenance work is well-resourced and routine, it should be rare for even major security updates to cause significant issues. What’s needed in the short term is a big investment in the people and training needed to roll out patches promptly and safely. What’s needed in the long term is a big investment in software security, eliminating entire classes of vulnerabilities, like memory safety, before they are ever written. For organizations that have gotten used to patching slowly and cautiously, suddenly switching gears to patching quickly is a big challenge. And the flood of vulnerability disclosures enabled by AI means that everyone is being asked to switch gears like that at once. Fortunately, it’s not a zero-sum game: patches can be rolled out quickly and cautiously, with investments in reducing technical debt and expanding maintenance budgets as described above. These measures are expensive and time-consuming, but necessary. For governments asking how to respond to AI-enabled cybersecurity threats, investing in the people and training necessary to stay on top of patches will pay big dividends in reliability and security. For individuals, consider the trade-offs when relying on a single provider for many services you rely on. Consumer cloud and device offerings tie together many of the things we need to function on a daily basis like email, messaging, file storage, and even payments, but that convenience and simplicity comes with the risk of losing access to it all if that service goes offline (or suspends your account ). Trying out interoperable alternatives is a great way to reduce your reliance on a single company. Finally, for any critical data, learn the 3-2-1 rule for backups: Keep three different copies on two different types of storage with one copy in a different physical location. For many users, a laptop or other personal device, cloud storage, and a local backup disk exemplify this rule, as long as the laptop stores data on its own drives, not only in the cloud. Among other things, the accelerated rollout of AI has made it all the more critical to reinvest in people and systems to keep our software, networks, governments, and interconnected world stable. *Apple is an EFF donor. articles.title: Deceptive Campaign Ballot Printing Sparks Urgent Australian Injunction
articles.content: An amended how-to-vote card distributed by Tosh-Jake Finnigan's campaign after a legal threat from the Greens. View image in fullscreen An amended how-to-vote card distributed by Tosh-Jake Finnigan's campaign after a legal threat from the Greens. Victorian Greens seek urgent injunction over how-to-vote cards mimicking party’s branding but preferencing it last Exclusive: Independent candidate Tosh-Jake Finnigan’s cards instruct people to vote in a way that would benefit Liberal party Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast The Victorian Greens are seeking an urgent injunction from the supreme court to stop an independent candidate distributing how-to-vote cards that allegedly mimic the party’s branding and urge people to preference it last. As prepoll opened on Wednesday morning, Tosh-Jake Finnigan’s campaign team handed out how-to-vote cards that used the minor party’s colour scheme, font and triangle logo with the banner “Vote 1 Green Values”. The card instructed people to vote in a way that would ultimately benefit the Liberal party. It asked voters to give their first preference to Finnigan followed by an Animal Justice party candidate, another independent candidate and then the Liberals in fourth place. The Greens are determined to win back the ultra-marginal seat it lost to the Liberals at a February 2025 byelection with a 1.3% margin. Labor is running an open ticket in Prahran, which the Greens fear could deprive it of the preference votes it needs . Steve Bracks is on board: Ben Carroll finds a believer as most write off Labor’s Victorian election chances Read more On Wednesday afternoon, the Greens state director, Martin Shield, requested Finnigan immediately stop distributing the material and threatened to take legal action if an undertaking was not given to do so in less than two hours. Finnigan agreed to the request and produced an amended how-to-vote card within hours that included different colours with a revised banner that said “Vote 1 Trans Greens Values”. View image in fullscreen A now destroyed how-to-vote card distributed by Tosh-Jake Finnigan’s campaign at prepoll on Wednesday morning. “Due to legal threats from the Greens party, I confirm that I am not an endorsed Greens party candidate,” a disclaimer on Finnigan’s revised how-to-vote card said. But the changes did not satisfy the Greens. On Friday afternoon, the party’s lawyers lodged papers in the supreme court. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email At an initial hearing on Friday night, the Greens’ lawyer, Adam McBeth, alleged people handing out Finnigan’s material at prepoll wore shirts with the exact shade of green as worn by genuine Greens party volunteers. McBeth alleged Finnigan’s team stood next to Greens party volunteers and Greens placards. The party argues voters at prepoll were deliberately misled. “There is no other reason for an independent candidate who has an infinite range of colours and styles to choose from to so closely mimic the Greens, including the way people paid to hand out were dressed and where they were directed to stand,” McBeth said. Finnigan, who was self-represented, said they had gone above and beyond to quickly make changes to their initial how-to-vote card and accused the Greens of using “legal manoeuvres” to stop them campaigning. “It is my belief that they don’t want me to hand out on Saturday, which will be one of the busiest days of prepoll,” Finnigan said. Finnigan told the court that they did not have enough money to print new cards. They said their campaign team had not been instructed to stand next to the Greens at prepoll. “I am someone who holds Greens values, of course I am going to have some kind of green shirt,” Finnigan said. “The honest reason I went for that colour of green is because the colour is called Irish green and I am of Irish background. That’s why I went for it. I just like the sound of Irish green.” On Friday evening, after the supreme court action was lodged, the Victorian Election Commission (VEC) accepted Finnigan’s subsequent how-to-vote card and published it online. Justice John Watson said the first how-to-vote card “looked like a pretty deliberate attempt to pass yourself off as a Greens candidate”, but he adjourned the matter until 3pm on Saturday to hear testimony from the VEC. Finnigan became Victoria’s first openly transgender councillor in 2023 when they were elected to the Colac Otway shire council after a countback. They resigned from the council in October 2024. The former Labor field campaigner founded the Restore Democracy Sack Dan Andrews party in 2022. They unsuccessfully contested an upper house seat for the party, securing 1% of first preference votes. After working in the offices of Labor ministers during the 2014 state campaign, Finnigan became a whistleblower in the so-called Red Shirts scandal, which saw taxpayer funds used to pay electorate officers campaigning for Labor. Finnigan’s campaign Facebook page carrying an authorisation message describes them as a “Green Independent” and contains attack ads against the minor party.
